clinical_category: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control

semantic_correction.stem: A client is preparing for discharge after total joint replacement. Which statement shows correct understanding of infection-related follow-up?

options.A: I will promptly report increasing redness, wound drainage, swelling, persistent or worsening joint pain, or fever to my healthcare team.
options.B: I can wait until the joint becomes unusable before reporting increasing redness or drainage because these are expected during recovery.
options.C: Once the incision closes, infection monitoring is no longer needed because implanted joint material cannot become infected later.
options.D: Persistent joint pain makes infection unlikely unless a high fever appears first, so I can continue routine follow-up.

semantic_correction.rationale: CDC identifies redness and pain around a surgical site, cloudy wound drainage, and fever as warning signs of surgical site infection and notes that infection can involve implanted material such as a hip replacement. AAOS joint-replacement guidance likewise instructs clients to notify the surgeon for increasing redness, tenderness or swelling, wound drainage, persistent fever or chills, and increasing joint pain. Infection can occur after discharge and does not require a high fever to precede local or pain-related findings. Therefore prompt reporting of new or worsening wound and joint findings is appropriate.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach clients after joint replacement to recognize and promptly report wound, joint, and systemic findings that may indicate surgical or prosthetic joint infection.
semantic_correction.source_organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC); American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons (AAOS)
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Surgical Site Infection Basics; Total Knee Replacement — Warning signs of infection
semantic_correction.source_version_date: CDC SSI Basics updated April 11, 2024; current AAOS OrthoInfo total-knee-replacement guidance accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: CDC SSI Basics — Types: infection may involve implanted material such as a hip replacement; Signs and symptoms: redness and pain around the surgical area, cloudy wound drainage, fever; once home, call provider immediately for infection symptoms. AAOS Total Knee Replacement — Warning signs of infection: persistent fever/chills, increasing redness/tenderness/swelling, wound drainage, increasing knee pain with activity and rest; tell doctor immediately
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: After joint replacement, increasing redness, drainage, swelling, worsening/persistent joint pain, or fever are infection warning signs that should be reported promptly; implanted material can be involved in SSI.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed 'only/always' distractor cueing, shortened the correct answer, and anchored follow-up teaching to current CDC and AAOS infection-warning signs without requiring high fever.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: CDC SSI Basics; AAOS Total Knee Replacement — Warning signs of infection
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control — postoperative infection recognition
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests practical post-discharge infection recognition and avoids implying that infection requires a high fever or ends when the incision closes.

option_audit.A: Correct. It reflects CDC and AAOS warning signs and prompt reporting guidance.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. Increasing redness or drainage should be reported rather than observed until major functional loss occurs.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Infection can involve implanted joint material and can present after discharge.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. A high fever is not required before local wound or joint findings become concerning.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone gives the appropriate reporting threshold without delaying for severe systemic illness.
cueing_check: All four choices are discharge follow-up statements of comparable length and specificity; no absolute-word or unique-length cue identifies A.
